In sum, I say that Andhra Pradesh, to which we belong, is suffering 
very badly. The people of Andhra Pradesh, the Congress Party, once again 
request the Central Government to release, immediately, the money as sought 
by the Government of Andhra Pradesh, i.e., Rs. 1810 crores. Then only one 
can say that the Central Government is doing justice for the people of Andhra 
Pradesh. 
Recently, all the Ministers of the State Governments met the Finance 
Minister, Shri Jaswant Singh. They explained the problem. Still, it is at the 
'thinking-level' only. I request the Gove rnment that in the coming Budget, it 
must provide sufficient money to meet the challenge of drought. It must work 
on a war-footing. Also, in the future Budgets, when they take money from 
institutions like the Asian Developm ent Bank or the World Bank or the 
international organisations or the Japa n Bank, they must give priority to 
constructing, immediately, some irrigation  projects in India, in various States. 
The Ganga-Cauvery link is only a dream project. It might need, perhaps, lakhs 
of crores of rupees. We will be happy if it comes about. Immediately, what they 
must do is, let them concentrate on constructing

 Pending projects for Rail Safety  
*61. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be -
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that several projects related to Rail safety in 
terms of track renewal rolling stock replacement/repair >f Railway bridges 
are pending; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof, date-wise and Zone-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): a) and 
(b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Renewal and replacement of tracks, bridges and rolling stock a 
continuous ongoing exercise. The works under these items are auctioned 
every year through the budget on the basis of laid down 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
criteria. For such replacements the sanctioned works are progressed and 
completed in a phased manner as per availability of funds and resources. 
As on 1.4.2002, the position of Track Renewal, Bridge works and 
Rolling Stock Programme has been as under: 
Track Renewal—Works are sanctioned for total 14,509 km. of track, 
out of which 4,000 km. is targeted for completion during 2002-2003. 
Bridges— A total of 4481 Nos. of bridges, including 527 distressed, are 
sanctioned and 1010 Nos. including 341 distressed bridges, are targeted for 
completion during the year 2002-03. 
Rolling Stock —No projects are pending for replacement of rolling 
stock, since rolling stock is not replaced based on projects but on the basis of 
Production Plan which is drawn up every year taking into account the 
fluctuations in traffic requirements and rolling stock replacement requirement 
on age cum condition basis. The actual production as per plan, is achieved on 
year to year basis. The figures, for the current year, are given below:

SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the detailed reply given 
by the hon. Railway Minister should actually be an eye-opener to the whole 
country because the kind of work that is remaining incomplete or unfinished 
is stupendous. The fact that we are not having more accidents of a fatal nature 
and some passengers are actually surviving the ordeal of journey on the 
Indian Railways is some kind of a mi racle. So far as track renewal is 
concerned, works were sanctioned for 14,509 km. of track, of which 4,000 
km. of track is targeted for completion during 2002-03. So far as the bridges 
which are to be repaired and renewed are concerned, sanction was given for 
4,481 bridges of which 1,010 bridges were targeted for completion during the 
year 2002-03. Apart from the accident involving the Howrah Rajdhani 
Express, many other train accidents have taken place. We are hearing almost 
on a daily basis that this or that train had a miraculous escape. At the last 
moment, something is identified; either there is some problem with the track 
or there is some problem with the bridge or there is some problem with the 
signal. The Khanna Committee which went into the question of railway safety 
in a big 
                                               3

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
way had made a number of recommendations. The main issue which was 
pointed out by the Khanna Committee was that there was no safety policy of 
the Railways. In such a situation, the Government of India made a major 
exception and Rs. 17,000 crores over a period of five years were earmarked 
for railway safety. Although this figure of Rs. 17,000 crores appears to be 
very impressive, but year-wise it is only Rs. 1,400 crores, Rs. 2,000 crores and 
so on. In this kind of a situation, the urgency or the importance that had to be 
shown by the Government in terms of reinforcing the safety measures, has not 
been shown. It is not that we do not have the resources or we cannot address 
the problem of safety wholly. But, the remaining part is very huge compared 
to the requirements. All other resources, which were available with the 
Railways, should have been diverted towards safety measures. My question is 
this. Woulcf the Government come up with a proper railway safety policy 
statement and also a White Paper along with an investment plan on an urgent 
basis, so that Parliament could have an opportunity to discuss it and 
recommend certain measures, thereby we are able to fulfil the safety 
requirements?

Central Teams have visited all the above States except Kerala. All the 
Teams have submitted their reports. In case of Kerala the State Government 
has been requested to furnish further information and clarifications. 
It is estimated that the loss of production in kharif foodgrains 
production will be of the order of 18.72 per cent. Shortage of fodder and 
drinking water is also being experienced in many States, States have taken 
many steps to deal with the situation including initiation of relief works, 
provision of drinking water including its transport through Rail in Rajasthan, 
setting up of fodder depots, remission of land revenue and in many cases 
stocking of foodgrains at the village level. Certain States have suspended 
recovery of co-operative dues and not resorting to coercive measures to effect 
recovery. Power supply for a minimum period and seed subsidy for growing 
fodder etc. are some other notable steps taken by the State Government.

Statement 
(a) to (e) Drought is a slow on-set phenomenon showing improvements 
and aggravations in its protracted course depending on occurrence of many 
events. Keeping these factors in view, it would be pre-mature to assess 
whether the assistance provided is adequate. 
So far, Rs. 1227.29 crores of Central share of the Calamity Relief 
Fund(CRF) for 2002-2003 and 19.25 lakh MTs of foodgrains for carrying out 
relief employment works have been sanctioned. Further, an amount of Rs. 
1999.14 crores has been found admissible for assistance from National 
Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) subject to adjustment of balances in the 
Calamity Relief Fund of the States. The situation will be further reviewed in 
middle of January to assess the requirements of further assistance. The 
relevant details are in the Statement-I (See below). 
Provision of relief on the ground is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments concerned. The Central Government supplements these 
.efforts. No specific complaints of relief not reaching the affected population 
have so far been received.

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
A Statement is laid pn the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a ) and (b) The low share of India's presence in the global trade of 
medicinal plants could be attributed to poor quality of produce, Unorganized 
production and marketing system, lack of awareness and inadequate 
database. A Task Force on Conservation and Sustainable Use of Medicinal 
Plants constituted by the Planning Commission has identified the following 
bottlenecks in the development of medicinal plants: 
1. The medicinal plants are collected mostly from the wild without 
paying attention to the stage of maturity, stored haphazardly for 
long period of time under unsuitable conditions thereby causing 
deterioration in the quality which are not acceptable to importers 
and standard drug manufacturing Units. 
2. The marketing of Medicinal Plants is inefficient, informal, 
secretive and opportunistic. As a result, raw material supply 
situation is shaky, unsustainable and exploitative. This results in 
depletion of resource base, exploitation of rural people, 
adulteration and non-availability of quality herbal drugs for 
domestic consumption as well as for exports. 
3. As forest.habitats disappear and overharvesting for  commercial 
use reduces the stocks of wild medicinal plant material, there is a 
corresponding drop in the availability of the plants normally used 
as the first and last resort for all health care by rural population. 
4. Despite the wealth of resources available, the sector has not 
developed owing to the absence of suitable standardization, 
quality control and efficacy of drugs. It has yet to formalize and 
organize marketing and trade and integrate the development of 
medicinal plants form production to consumption to boost export 
of herbal formulations. 
29 

RAJYA  SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
5. The medicinal plants sector has a number of stakeholders having 
divergent interests. There is lack of coordination and each 
stakeholder is interested in strengthening specific aspects of his 
sector only and ignoring the overall development. 
6. Several constraints exist due to inadequate awareness; inadequate 
investments in research and development; manufacturer — 
exporter dissonance; lack of quality and standardization norms; 
and lack of adequate marketing and trade information. 
The Central Government have taken various initiatives to promote 
Research and Development of medicinal plants in the country including 
creation of infrastructure for quality testing. The following agencies are 
involved in encouraging the farmers to use the latest technologies for getting 
higher yield and deriving higher income: 
(i) The National Research Centre on Medicinal and Aromatic Plants, 
Anand, Gujarat under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research 
(ICAR) is carrying out research work exclusively on medicinal 
and aromatic plants. 
(ii) Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and its 
constituent laboratories including Central Institute of Medicinal 
and Aromatic Plants (CIMAP) are also carrying our research 
activities for the development of these plants. 
(iii) Department of Agriculture and Cooperation, Ministry of 
Agriculture is implementing developmental programmes on 
medicinal and aromatic plants through Plan Scheme to address the 
issues of quality planting material, conservation of germplasm, 
coverage of area under improved varieties and quality assessment 
through Regional Analytical Laboratories. 
(iv) National Medicinal Plants Board, Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare is implementing various programmes in an integrated  
manner and is overseeing the  overall

International decade for culture of peace and non-violence 
*64. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU) : Will the 
Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in view of the United Nations' declaring 2001—2010 as the 
International decade for a culture of peace and non-violence for the children 
of the World, Government have drawn out elaborate programmes for the 
children of India; and 
32 

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken or proposed to be taken 
in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) The General Assembly of the 
United Nations proclaimed the year 2000 as the "International Year for the 
Culture of Peace" and the decade 2001—2010 as the uInternational Decade 
for the Promotion of a Culture of Peace and Non-Violence for the Children of 
the World'. UNESCO was entrusted with the task of mobilizing Member 
States and Associate Members and co-ordinating the programme and activities 
of the United Nations Agencies and other International Organizations. 
Accordingly UNESCO requested all National Commissions to undertake a 
series of activities which could contribute to spreading the message of 'Culture 
of Peace'. The year was formally launched world wide on 14.9.1999 which 
was the opening day of the last Session of the UN General Assembly in the 
20th Century and was designated as International day of Peace. 
The Culture of Peace and Non-Violence is not something new to our 
country. Bearing this in mind, The Indian National Commission launched the 
year with a function where Education Secretary gave an address on 'Culture of 
Peace' and the famous classical dancer Ms. Sonal Mansingh gave a 
performance on the theme of Peace before an International audience and the 
guests signed the Culture of Peace manifesto. All-the State Governments, 
Associated Schools, UNESCO Clubs, Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and 
Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan were also requested to organize activities on 
the Culture of Peace and to sign the Culture of Peace Manifesto. The 
Manifesto was also signed by the Prime Minister at a simple ceremony at 
P.M. House. Apart from the activities undertaken by the State Governments, 
Associated Schools, UNESCO Clubs, Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and 
Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan a major International Youth Forum on 
Cultural Heritage was jointly organized from 28th December, 2000 to 2nd 
January, 2001 by the Indian National Commission and the Delhi Public 
School, R. K. Puram. In addition, the Indian National Commission organized 
10 Workshops on the Culture of Peace at Gurgaon, Faridabad, Shimla, 
Dehradun, Jammu, Patna, Kolasib, Bhopal, Pataudi and Delhi with a view to 
associating 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
the NGOs, students and UNESCO Clubs etc. with the Culture of Peace 
movement. 
On the recommendation of the Indian National Commission the 
Brahma Kumar’s signed an agreement with UNESCO for participation in the 
movement. By employing a Task Force of four thousands volunteers over a 
period of 7 months they collected over 35 million signatures in India alone 
for the Manifesto of Culture of Peace. 
A UNESCO Chair on Culture of Peace and Non-Violence has been 
functioning since 1999 at the Manipal Academy of Higher Education, 
Manipal. 
As regards the "International Decade for the Promotion of a Culture of 
Peace and Non-Violence for the Children of the World' each year is required 
to be marked with a different priority and for 2001, UNESCO had suggested 
that the emphasis be given to the United Nations Year of Dialogue among 
Civilizations and the International year of Mobilization against Racism, 
Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and related Intolerance. During the 
UNESCO's General Conference held in October-November, 2001 the 
President of the Indian National Commission conveyed India's intention to 
organize an International Conference on Dialogue among Civilizations, which 
was accepted by the Director General. Further details for organizing the 
Conference are being worked out. 
The Commission is organising a series of lectures in connection with 
the "International Decade for the Promotion of a Culture of Peace and Non-
Violence for the Children of the World'. Two such lectures-one by His 
Holiness the Dalai Lama and the other by Acharya Vidyanandji Muniraj were 
organized during the last year. 
The City Montessori School, Lucknow has been awarded the UNESCO 
Prize for Peace Education for 2002 "in recognition of its efforts to promote 
the universal values of education for peace and tolerance and to renew the 
principles of secularism at a time when these values and principles are 
increasingly being challenged."

(c) what are the suggestions made by the Indian Government in the 
above Convention; and 
(d) whether Government propose to implement it? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T .R. 
BAALU) (a) to (d) The Eighth Conference of the Parties to the United Nations 
Framework Convention on Climate Change was held recently in New Delhi 
from 23rd October to 1st November 2002. The Delhi Ministerial Declaration 
on Climate Change and Sustainable Development issued at the end of the 
Conference establishes the link between climate change and sustainable 
development and brings into focus the issue of adaptation to the adverse 
effects of climate change. The Conference advanced operationalisation of 
Special Climate Change Fund and Least Developed Countries Fund for providing 
financial resources to developing countries. The Conference also concluded 
three years of negotiations relating to reporting and review under the Kyoto 
Protocol and rules of procedure of Executive Board of the Clean Development 
Mechanism as well as simplified modalities and procedures for small-scale 
Clean Development Mechanism projects. It also adopted the New Delhi Work 
programme relating to education, training and public awareness about issues 
relating to climate change. 
A group of developed countries wanted to initiate a process for 
beginning a dialogue on broader participation of countries in greenhouse 
92 

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
gas mitigation commitments for period beyond 2012. This was resisted 
successfully by the developing countries, including India, on the grounds that the 
per capita greenhouse gas emissions of the developing countries, in general, were 
low in comparison to the developed countries, and that the overriding priority for 
the developing countries was poverty eradication for which economic growth 
was essential. A framework of legislative and policy measures are in place in 
India that would help in minimizing the causes of climate change. Several 
measures have already been implemented by the Government of India to 
promote efficient utilization of fossil fuels, use of renewable energy 
technologies, abatement of pollution and conservation of forests. 
Johannesburg Earth Summit 
373. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the major issues considered by the UN World Summit on 
Sustainable Development (the Earth Summit) held in Johannesburg recently; 
(b) the assessment of the progress made on various issues since the last 
Summit at Rio de Janeiro in 1992, with highlights of the contentious issues 
involved and the Indian view point thereon; and 
(c) the final resolutions adopted by the Summit and the follow up action 
required to be taken by India? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU) (a) World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD) acted as a 
10-year review of the United Nations Conference on Environment and 
Development (UNCED) process and identified major accomplishments and 
obstacles in implementing Agenda 21. The major issues considered by the 
WSSD, inter-alia, include poverty eradication, changing unsustainable patterns 
of consumption and production, protecting and managing the natural resource 
base of economic and social development, sustainable development in a 
globalizing world, health and sustainable development, sustainable 
development of small island developing countries, means of implementation 
and institutional framework for sustainable development. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
(b) The major outcome of the Summit was that it reaffirmed 
"sustainable development" as a central element of the international 
agenda and gave a new impetus on global action to fight poverty and 
protect the environment. The understanding of sustainable development 
was broadened and strengthened as a result of the Summit, particularly 
important linkages between poverty, the environment and the use of 
natural resources were clearly established. As a result of a coordinated 
approach adopted by the developing countries including India, in addition 
to reiterating Millennium Development Goals and objectives of various 
multilateral environment agreements the Summit agreed on: 
(i) Increasing the number of people with access to clean water and 
sanitation facilities by half by the year 2015. 
(ii) Reducing the proportion of people without access to cleaner energy 
by the year 2015. 
(iii) Helping the developing countries with necessary resources to 
increase the share of renewable energy in a gradual manner. 
(iv) Evolving an international regime to ensure fair and equitable 
sharing of benefits arising from the use of genetic resources in a 
transparent manner. 
(v) Developed Countries to take lead in shifting away from the present 
pattern of unsustainable consumption and production. 
(vi) Successfully countered the efforts made by various blocks on 
imposing disguised trade barriers in the nature of eco-labeling, life-
cycle analysis criteria, and inclusion of core labour standards of ILO. 
(c) The Plan of Implementation and Political Declaration issued 
after the Summit has highlighted concerns of developing countries and 
reflect consensus among all countries arrived after the WSSD. The Plan 
of Implementation calls for immediate international action to tackle 
these issues. The Government regularly monitors its performance on 
the benchmark of annual and Five Year Plans which contain all elements 
of sustainable development. Ministry of Environment and Forests has 
set up a mechanism for follow up action on various decisions taken in 
the World Summit.

CHAPTER 4 
Modernisation of Signal and Telecommunication System 
4. Highlights 
 The Standing Committee on Railways (1996) viewed that the

Railways should be made a thrust area for investment in IXth Plan 
(1997—2002). However, during the period from 1996-97 to 2000-01, 
out of the total allocation of Rs. 58010.96 crore on nine Zonal 
Railways for Grant No. 16—Assets, Acquisition, Construction and 
Replacement, the allocation for S&T was only Rs. 1482.02 crore, a 
mere 2.55 per cent. 
(Para 6) 
146 

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
 Modernisation of points and signals through Panel Interlocking . 
(PI), Route Relay Interlocking (RRI) and Solid State Interlocking 
(SSI) had not been completed. Out of 5244 signalling stations, 
only 1812,180 and 13 stations respectively were provided with 
PI, RRI and SSI and 3093 stations were still being operated 
mechanically. In 431 out of 1075 stations on 'A' route, points 
and signals are still being operated through mechanical means. 
(Para 7.1) 
 Out of 6746.73 route Km, automatic signalling was in use only for a 
limited length i.e. in 560.34 route Kms. on 'A' route and work was 
stated to be in progress on 170 route Kms. No concrete steps had been 
taken to introduce modern signalling system on remaining 6016.39 
route Kms. of 'A' route. 
(Para 7.2)

railways, where the utilization of line capacity is more than 100% 
automatic block signalling has not been provided to de-congest the 
traffic. 
(Para 7.2.1.1) 
 Sanction for construction of 3rd line was accorded during the 
review period in 8 sections on three Zonal Railway at a cost of

increase cogld have been achieved by provision of automatic 
block signalling at an estimated cost of Rs. 61.42 crores. 
(Para 7.2.1.2) 
 Due to line capacity constraints, traffic on 17 routes is being 
moved through longer routes for mo re than five years. In respect 
of 8 routes, rationalization orders were in force for more than 10

Experiments about monsoon failure 
449. SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Indian Meteorological Department's experts have 
examined the causes for the failure of the just concluded summer monsoon in 
the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the results of experiment conducted jointly by several 
organisations in the Arabian Sea between June, 15 and August, 15 to gather 
ocean and atmospheric observations have been examined; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the measures to be adopted for long range month-wise 
prediction of the Monsoon in future? 
157 

RAJYA  SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY ( SHRI BHACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) to (e) The Indian 
Meteorological Department has examined the causes of failure of this year's 
monsoon. This year, the onset of the southwest monsoon over Kerala was on 
time (29 May). It covered peninsular India, northeast region and some parts of 
east central India by middle of June, as per its normal pattern. The rainfall 
activity was normal (+7%) during June. This was caused mainly by the 
development of a low pressure area that moved westward across central parts 
of the country. Thereafter, there was delay in its further progress. Dry spells 
and breaks in the monsoon are the normal features of the monsoon system. 
This year, however, the break in the monsoon developed even before its 
advance over north/northwest India resulting in prolonged dry summer 
conditions. The details of the failure of Monsoon 2002 are as follow:— 
(i) The delay in the progression of monsoon was due to the presence 
of an anomalous anticyclonic flow/descending motion over 
western parts of country. 
(ii) Heavy rainfall events are in association with monsoon depressions 
which develop over Bay of Bengal during monson season. Not a 
single monsoon depression formed during this season as against 
the normal of 5-6 depressions per season. 
(iii) Most of low pressure areas formed during the season we/e quite 
feeble. They were short lived and moved along the seasonal 
trough. 
(iv) The seasonal/monsoon trough itself had been quite weak and was 
located close to foothills of Himalayas for a long time in July. 
(v) The cross equatorial flow in the Arabian Sea as well as in the Bay 
of Bengal was extremely weak. Cloud system moved towards 
pacific Ocean particularly during the month of July and in the 
second half of September. 
158 

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(vi) The El-Nino showed an anomalous behaviour in that, it weakened 
over the area off Peru coast during monsoon season but 
strengthened over West Pacific Ocean. 
The Department of Science and Technology (DST) is coordinating the 
Arabian Sea Monsoon Experiment (ARMEX) under Indian Climate Research 
Programme (ICRP) in two phases. The first phase was organised from 15 
June to 15 August this year with the participation of a large number of 
national organisations. In order to understand development of small scale 
heavy rain producing systems associated with Offshore trough/vortex 
attempts were made to gather atmospheric and oceanic observations which 
were maximised during 'Intensive Observation Period'. These observations are 
being currently analysed by all the participating agencies. The second phase 
of ARMEX will be conducted from mid March to mid May 2003, in which 
observations will be collected to understand the development and collapse of 
warm pool in southeast Arbian Sea. The total picture will emerge only after 
the second phase is over. 
Action has been initiated to develop the forecast models for the month-
wise prediction of monsoon rainfall.

which as all of us know is many areas they have all been taken over and 
houses have been constructed in the rural areas also. We have to consider 
both these things. As the Prime Minister had announced in the Lok Sabha, a 
scheme of linking rivers is under the activities consideration of the 
Government. We will look into it. Money will not be a hindrance in 
implementing that plan, if that can be done technically. 
I come back to the PDS and other things. Let me make one thing very 
clear. The Central Government can only have schemes and can give money. 
The Central Government has no implementing agency. We do not have 
patwaris; we do not have SDMs and we do not have District Collectors under 
our control. We have no implementing agency and monitoring agency. After 
all, they are democratically elected Governments. We can give them money. 
We can give them assistance. We can tell them what to do. But it is their right 
to decide how they should use that money and how effectively they should 
spend that money. Therefore, if you say that the Central Government should 
be held responsible if food is not distributed properly or if the money 
intended does not reach the people for whom it is intended. I don't think in 
our federal system that is the right way of putting things. 
Many hon. Members wanted that the elected representatives should be 
associated with the draught relief work. This demand was

merchants of Thiruvannamalai, it should be prevented.

the temple. They want to worship the deity, the sanctum. In Tamil Nadu, at 
Valluvarkottam, the statue of Valluvar, Pomhukkar, Kannagi are being 
neglected. The Archaeological Survey of India is taking steps to take this 
temple in its custody. Therefore, it is requested that respecting the sentiments 
of the people of Tamil Nadu, the hon. Prime Minister should intervene in the 
matter and prevent this from happening.

countries. Such violence continues to cut across culture,

class, education, income, ethnicity and age. Domestic violence is one of the most

Sir, the domestic violence in India is no less than cancer or any other 
ailment. But there is no law to protect its victims. Not a day passes when

SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN (Nominated): Thank you, Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir. I will just take a few minutes, not only to welcome this Private 
Member's Bill, but also to emphasise to all the Members in this House that the 
right to the matrimonial home, what is called the shared household, as the Bill 
describes it, is the most important insurance against domestic violence. This 
concept, Sir, was an invention, originally, of Judges in England. After the War, 
when half a million soldiers did not come back because they were killed in 
France, Germany etc., there were a large number of widows in England who 
were subjected to eviction proceedings. These eviction proceedings resulted 
in eviction orders, because the tenant was only the husband and since there 
were no prospects of the husband coming back, the court said: "An eviction 
order has to go, as a matter of course." So, thousands and thousands 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
of widows were evicted, and it was only because of the ingenuity of a 
great Judge, Lord Denning, particularly, who invented this concept of a 
matrimonial home that the women were saved. He said that the 
matrimonial home is a concept which we must now introduce in society, 
namely, the husband and the wife share a home and therefore, this 
shared household concept came in. Unfortunately, this decision was 
reversed by the House of Lords. They said: "When we look at the law, 
there is no such thing here," and there was such an uproar in Parliament 
that they had to introduce a Bill, which became the Matrimonial Homes 
Act. Therefore, Sir, I very strongly recommend to the hon. Minister to 
consider that in the Government-int roduced Bill, where this clause is 
absent. It is a very, very important protection, almost a certain insurance, 
against domestic violence, and I would respectfully request the 
Government to kindly introduce this concept in such form as they think 
right, because it is time we introduced it. It was introduced long ago in 
the European countries. We must now introduce it in our society. 
Secondly, the term domestic violence as the hon. Member, Mr. Santosh 
Bagrodia, when he spoke from the floor said, was inadequately defined. 
Right. It was inadequately defined, but I would respectfully suggest, let 
us not reinvent the wheel. It has been considered very carefully and the 
U.N. Model Code of Conduct on Violence defines domestic violence. 
So, I would respectfully suggest that, as far as possible, we adopt that 
provision to our definition of domestic violence because it covers a 
very wide variety of different types of violence. It is correct that we 
require a change in the mindset because we are a male-dominated 
society. But laws do help and laws do bring about a social change and 
help establish norms of behaviour. And ultimately we must try to break 
this chain of violence where the frustrations of a daughter-in-law lead 
to a dominant mother-in-law, who herself becomes violent to her daughter-
in-law in turn because that is also a type of violence that we have to 
eschew, that we have to prevent and that requires certainly, as one of 
the honourable Members rightly said, education in our society, in this 
particularly male-dominated society. But I would respectfully urge that 
even if the honourable Minister does not accept all the provisions of 
this Bill, the two most important provisions are: (1) The proper definition 
of 'domestic violence', and (2) The right to a shared household, 
howsoever you put it, or a matrimonial home. Thank you.

The Constitution (Amendment) Bill, 1999 (Insertion of 
 New Article 21A) 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Sir, I move:— 
"That the Bill further to amend the Constitution of India, be taken into 
consideration". 
Sir, for a human being, privacy is very important factor. Today, what is 
happening is that, whoever is the authority, just gets into your house thinking 
that they can take advantage of a particular clause of a Bill. It is so 
unfortunate that on flimsy grounds, on mere assumptions, they get into your 
houses; not only your houses, but the houses of your relations, distant 
relations, distant friends. I also know that in some cases, these authorities have 
entered our multi-storeyed building, going into every flat of the multi-storeyed 
building. Now, that is not privacy. After all, the dignity of an individual 
should be respected. We are in a society where freedom is very important. And 
If my privacy is hampered, if my privacy is questioned, then it becomes a 
police raj. It would mean as if we are in a situation where the entire country is 
made of scoundrels. And it is only the officers, only the bureaucrats, only a 
small number of intelligence officers or other officers in different departments, 
economic or other departments, who are most honest, who are absolutely 
above board. This is not fair. This has to be looked into by the Government very 
seriously to see how we can protect the dignity of an ordinary citizen. I know 
a number of people, a number of officers just getting into somebody's house, 
saying that they have got the right, that they will bring out some paper, etc. It 
has been noticed that, sometimes they sign the warrant on the spot, and when 
they enter, they donl allow the people to take the help of the lawyers. An 
ordinary citizen is not supposed to be an expert lawyer; he is not an expert on 
law matters. He is told "No, sorry", because that is the only way you can 
threaten him.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. 
RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Ministry of Water Resources has reported that the Central 
Ground Water Board (CGWB) under that Ministry has implemented a 
Central Sector Scheme for 'Study of Recharge to Ground Water' during Ninth 
Five Year Plan. Under the Scheme, artificial recharge projects were taken up 
in the country, including in some Metro cities, the details of which are given 
in the Annexure. [See Appendix 197 Annexure no. 4] 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri K. Rahman Khan. 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
The CGWB has proposed a Central Sector Scheme on "Development of 
Ground Water Resources and Rain Water Harvesting in Majo r Cities" at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 20.00 crore for inclusion in the Tenth Five Year Plan. 
17 major capital cities, viz. Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai. Kolkata, Hyderabad, 
Guwahati, Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhubaneshwar. Jaipur, Lucknow, 
Bhopal, Patna, Raipur, Ranchi, Thiruvananthapuram and Chandigarh are 
proposed to be included in this scheme. This proposed scheme is still at a 
consultation stage. 
The CGWB has prepared  and circulated Manual and Guidelines on 
Artificial Recharge to Ground Water to all States/Union Territories 
incorporating various modern techniques of rain water harvesting for 
adoption. The Board also organi zed mass awareness and training 
programmes on rain water harvesting all over the country. A website oh Roof 
Top Rain Water Harvesting (www. cgwb india.com) has also been launched 
to make aware and educate the public about various techniques of harvesting 
rain water and store it for future us e. The Board also provides technical 
guidance to Individuals/organizations/ in dustries to adopt efficient recharge 
system through out the country. 
The Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation has also 
circulated the literature/guidelines on rain water harvesting provided by the 
Ministry of Water Resources/CGWB to all State/UT Chief Secretaries and 
Secretaries in-charge of urban water supply for adoption in those areas where 
there has been sharp decline in the ground water level. State Governments 
have also been advised to make a beginning in the existing Government 
offices/buildings housing complexes and to make it mandatory for all new 
building by amending the building bye-laws. In Delhi, the Ministry has 
issued a notification on 28.7.2001 for modification/addition in the building 
Bye-laws, 1983 which makes it mandatory for water harvesting through 
storing of water runoff including rain water in all new buildings on plots of 
100 sq. mtrs and above.

DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether It has come to the notice of Government that an independent 
survey conducted by a prom inent national daily, r ecently throws up several

30

(c) whether it is a fact that the sample of Delhi Jal Board has failed in the

an outbreak of typhoid amongst its doctors; and

THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI ANANTH KUMAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Delhi Jal Board has reported that the amount of Total Dissolved 
Solids (TDS) and Total Hardness in the water supplied by It are well within 
permissible limits prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards {IS-10500-
1993) and by the Central Public Health and Environmental Engineering 
Organisation (CPHEEO), Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty 
Alleviation, Govt, of India. The water is adequately disinfected and free 
Chlorine residual at level of 0.2 to 0.5 mg/1 is maintained at the consumer's 
end. 
(c) Delhi Jal Board is supplying filtered water in bulk to AIIMS. The 
AltMS authorities are mixing water from tubewells locally installed and 
operated by them. 
The News-item in this regard appeared in the Hindustan Times dated 
1.9.2002. Consequently the matter was investigated by Director {Treatment 
and Quality Control), Delhi Jal Board. A total of 120 samples were lifted and 
water of all the samples was found to be having sufficient free residual 
chlorine. 
(d) Delhi Jal Board is taking following preventive and remedial 
steps to provide potable water:— 
(i) Regular surveillance of quality of water is done by lifting and 
testing the water samples right from raw water Intake upto 
consumer's end. About 300 winter samples are lifted daily and 
tested by Six well-equipped Laboratories. 
(ii) 140 MGD Water Treatment Plant is being set up at Sonia Vihar 
Trans Yamuna Area and targeted to be completed by December, 
2003 
(iii) A regular survey is being d one to replace old corroded/ leaking 
water mains.

Control of health hazard environment 
*89. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that a disgusting mixture of smoke and fog 
(smog) is keeping pollutants, especially suspended particulate matter and 
pollen at breathing level, causing widespread viral infection, Asthma etc. in 
most parts of North and some parts of Western India; and 
(b) if so, the measures, so far, take n or are being contemplated by 
Government so that this health hazar d environment could be controlled and 
adequate medical care in the shape of prevention and treatment is taken? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) It has been a general observation that during 
the winter season, including the smoggy conditions, the levels of Suspended 
Particulate Matter (SPM) are comparatively 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
higher than during the other seasons. The SPM affects the respiratory system 
and may cause Asthma and viral infection. Studies conducted by Vallabha 
Bhai Pate! Chest Institute. New Delhi, and National Institute of Occupational 
Health, Ahmedabad, have shown some relationship between air pollution and 
respiratory diseases. 
(b) The present health care infrastructure  at the Centre and State levels is 
geared to meet the needs of the pe ople suffering from viral infections. 
Asthma etc. However, as part of pr eventive measures, the Government has 
already Implemented certain control measures such as introduction of:— 
(i) Unleaded petrol 
(ii) Bharat I & II emission standards 
(iii) Low Sulphur Diesel 
(iv) CNG for commercial vehicles 
(v) Pollution Under Control (PUC) Certificate. 
Central Pollution Control Board, Delhi, is the authority for checking the 
air pollution levels in various cities and for studying the effects of various 
control measures through the State Pollution Control Boards.

(c) The term state-of-the-art system to monitor ship traffic is 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
usually applied to the system that monitors ship traffic to ensure safe navigation 
of ships at Port channels. Vessel Traffi c Management System (VTMS) is a radar 
surveillance system broadly intended for providing effective guidance to pilotage 
of incoming and outgoing vessels. The radar surveillance system has a 
communication network with centers of Port activities controlling traffic 
movement. The system is designed to identify a medium-sized vessel, to compute 
the positional fixings along the shipping channel, to track all targets, mobile and . 
stationary, which are automa tically projected in th^scr een. to compute mobile 
target speed, course and absolute movement along the shipping channel and to 
forecast expected time of arrival and u pdate all Information every second with 
access to and from the different control points. 
VTMS facilities are presently availabl e at Kolkata, Mumbal, Jawahar Lai 
Nehru, Mormugao and New Mangalore Ports. The installation of VTMS at 
Kandia Port has been taken up in the Gulf of Kutch, jointly by this Port, Gujarat 
Maritime Board and the Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships. 
Paradip Port has decided to take up the installation of VTMS during the 10"^ Plan 
period considering the level of traffic in the Port and cost involved. The facility of 
VTMS has not been felt necessary at Visakhapatnam, Chennai, Cochin, Tuticorin 
and Ennore Ports.

Report of Law Commission on judicial arrears 
*100. SHRI SURENDRA UTH: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Law Commission headed by Justice M. Jagannadha Rao 
has submitted its report on judicial arrears; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken by Government to reduce the backlog of 
cases? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHY): (a) and (b) The Law Commission has informed that the 
present (Sixteenth) Law Commission headed by Justice M. Jagannadha Rao 
has neither submitted any report on "Judicial arrears", nor any project, at 
present, is pending on the subject. 
(c) Both the Government and the Judi ciary are concerned with the quick 
disposal of pending cases. Various steps have been taken by the Government 
for speeding up the disposal of these cases. These include simplification of rules 
and procedures on the basis of the advice and recommendations of expert 
bodies, like the Law Commission, the Malimath Committee etc. 
Further, the Government have also been constantly reviewing the 
accumulation of arrears in courts. Besides, increasing the judge-strength from 
time to time, the Government have set up/encouraged alternative modes of 
dispute-resolution, including conciliation, mediation and arbitration. Special 
tribunals, like Central Administrative Tribunal, State Administrative Tribunals 
Income Tax Appellate Trib unal, Labour Courts etc. have been set up to 
expedite disposal of cases. Inform ation Technology is being used in 
generation of cause list, providing 
55 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
information to the litigants/advocates et c. for speedy disposal of cases. Pilot 
project for the district courts has been started for computerization of city civil 
courts in the four major metro cities of Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai. 
All Central Ministries/ Departments have  been requested to take necessary 
steps like review of Acts/laws, administered by them, filing of counter-
affidavit in time and avoidance of unnecessary adjournment of cases. 
Fast Track Courts have been set up for quick disposal of long pending 
cases, priority being accorded to sessi ons cases pending for 2 years or more 
and cases involving underthals in jails. 
Civil Procedure Code has been amended and the amendments have been 
brought into force w.e.f. 1.7.2002, which include limit the number of 
adjournments which can be granted to a party to three, provide for speedy 
process service by speed post, courier se rvices, FAX or Email, authorize the 
court to fix time limit for oral arguments and provide for a number of other 
measures aimed at ensuring expeditious disposal. 
The Minister of Law & Justice has been addressing the High Courts 
periodically for filling up of vacancies of Judges in the Hi gh Courts. Efforts 
are also being made to adopt alternative modes of dispute resolution, such as, 
arbitration, conciliation and settlement of cases through Lok Adalats.

New patent regime 
457. SHRI R PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned, "Patent regime unlikely to benefit developing nations: UK 
58 

(25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Report", which appeared in the Economic Times, dated the 20"^ September. 
2002; 
(b) if so. the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the details of steps Government propose to take with regard to the 
n^ajor problems highlighted in the report so as to adequately safeguard the 
interests of the developing countries esoeeially India in the new patent 
regime? 
THE fyllNISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The 
Commission on Intellectual Property Rights was set up by the British 
Government with a view to  consider (a) how nation al intellectual property 
regimes could best be designed to benefit developing countries within the 
context of internationa l agreements, including the agreement on Trade 
Related Aspects of Intellectual Property; (b) how the international 
framework of rules and agreements might be improved and developed; and 
(c) the broader policy framework needed to complement intellectual property 
regimes. 
The report which seeks to integrate intellectual property rights and 
development policy, neither negates nor invalidates the utility of the 
intellectual property system per se for developing countries. 
It does, however, emphasise the need for adequate safeguards in the 
patent laws of developing countries. The main safeguards suggested in 
respect of patent regimes relate to: compulsory licensing; parallel imports; 
Government use of patent; exclusion of diagnostic, therapeutic and surgical 
methods from patentability; exclusion of new uses of known products from 
patentability; Bolar provision; prohibition of patent protection on plants and 
animals including genes and genetically modified plants and animals; and an 
obligation to disclose the geographical source of the genetic resources used 
in invention in the patent applications. The Patents Act, 1970 as amended by 
the Patents (Amendment) Act, 2002 substantially provides for these 
safeguards along with provisions which, in sum, enable an appropriate, 
timely and efficient response to national and public interest 
requirements/concerns.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE {SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) Regulation of the 
production of the Genetically Modified Crops Including environmental 
release has been laid down under statutory provision of Environmental 
Protection Act, 1986. Under the rule of the manufacture, use, Import and 
Storage of Hazardous Mi ro-organisms/Genetically Engineered Organizers or 
cell, 1989 notified under the Environmental Act, 1986 food s t u f f ,  
ingredients in food stuffs and additives including processing aids containing 
or consisting or genetically engineered organisms or cells shall not be 
produced, sold, imported or used except with the approval of the Genetic 
Engineering Approvals Committee- 
The Genetically Modified products that  are currently in the international 
market have to pass risk assessment conducted by national authorities of the 
countries where they are permitted. As per the WHO, the safety assessment 
of Genetically Modified foods generally investigate (a) direct health effects 
(toxicity); (b) tendencies to provoke allergic reaction (allergenicity): (c) 
specific components thought to have nutritional or toxic properties; (d) the 
stability of the inserted gene; (e) nutri tional effects associated with genetic 
modification; and (f) any unintended effects which could result from the gene 
insertion. 
All genetically modified foods are evaluated for health risk. The Maize 
variety "Starlink" developed in the USA was one such genetically Modified 
crop that was withdrawn from the market in USA and Japan because of 
suspected health risk. In India only BT cotton has been permitted, after 
extensive tests and risk assessments, to be commercially produced and 
marketed.

Dear Shri 
As you are kindly aware, Central Government adopted the National 
Population Policy in February 2000 with an objective of achieving stable 
population, nationally, by 2045. For attaining this objective it is necessary to 
achieve certain socio-demographic indicators by 2010, 
108 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
which will pave the way for stable population. Among the major goals for 
2010 are:— 
1. To meet the demands in full for basic reproductive and child 
health services, supplies and infrastructure. 
2. Reducing infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1000 live births. 
3. Reducing maternal mortality to below 100 per one lakh live 
births. 
4. Achieving universal immunization of children against all vaccine 
preventable diseases. 
5. Achieving 80% institutional deliveries and 100% deliveries by 
trained persons. 
6. Increasing use of contraceptives w ith a wide basket of choices.
  
7. Achieving 100% registration of births, deaths, marriages and 
pregnancies 
8. Integrating Indian system of Medicines  in providing 
reproductive and child health services. 
9. Promoting small family norm to achieve replacement levels of 
fertility by 2010. 
 
10. Making school education up to age 14 free and compulsory and 
reduce drop out at primary and secondary school levels. 
11. Promoting delayed marriage for girls. 
12. Bringing about convergences in im plementation of related social 
sector programmes so that fami ly welfare becomes a people's 
centered programme. 
To achieve the above goals emphas is should be laid on focused 
campaigns, evolving good management practices and strengthening 
provision of services and supplies at the grass roots level. Effective 
decentralization of services to Panchayat Raj bodies involvement of NGOs 
and private sector in creation of awareness and effecting service delivery are 
essential strategies which need to be adopted by the States. 
Since, there are vast disparities among the States in the achievement of 
the ssocio-demographic indicators, the strategies for 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
implementation of the programmes have to be different. Some States like 
Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Goa have already achieved replacement level of fertility. 
They have to devise programmes for sustainability and enhanced investment 
in human beings for improving the quality of lives that people lead. On the 
other hand, States like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, 
Chattisgarh, Jharkhand and Orissa have to implement the programmes of 
family welfare and reproductive and child health more vigorously, in order to 
increase the outreach of supplies and services for promoting small family 
norm. The Central Government has set up an Empowered Action Group to 
assist these States (Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Orissa, 
Uttaranchal, Jharkhand and Chattisgarh), which have, so far, lagged behind, 
in socio-demographic achievements in devising focused programmes for 
improving the situation there. 
Some of the State Governments like Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya 
Pradesh, R^asthan and Gujarat have al ready formulated th eir State specific 
population policies and other State Governments have initialed action for 
developing their population policies. This is a welcome step. This reflects the 
commitment of the State Governments towards population stabilization and 
sustainable development. 
It may be noted in this conext that National Population Policy affirms the 
commitment of the Government towards voluntary and informed choice and 
consent of citizens while availing re productive health care services and 
continuation of target free approach in  administering family welfare services. 
The,NPP-2000 provides a policy framework for advancing goals and 
prioritizing strategies during the next decade, to meet the reproductive and 
child health needs of the people of India and to achieve net replacement levels 
by 2010. It is based upon the need to simultaneously address issues of child 
survival, immunization, maternal hea lth and contraception while increasing 
outreach and coverage of a comprehensive package of reproductive and child 
health services by Government, industry and the voluntary, Non-Government 
sector, working in partnership. Impos ing arbitrary targ ets on contraception 
like sterilization, lUDs etc. reflects a 'topdown' approach, which goes against 
decentralized planning and service delivery and denies people the right to 
informed choice. Instead, a Community Needs Assessment Approach which 
aggregates the level of expectations of performance from the field into an 
achievable and quantified goal will be a more suitable strategy for population 
stabilization. 
110 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
In view of these basic principles, the National Population Policy does not 
provide for any individual  incentives or disincenti ves, because incentives 
always look small and distort response of citizens while on the other hand 
disincentives tend to be coercive. It has also been noticed that the 
disincentives always hit the poor and down trodden especially those who 
belong to scheduled castes and tribes and backward classes much harder than 
the privileged sections of society. Till the large unmet needs of those socially 
backward groups for health and family welfare services are met, proposing 
and puritive measures is clearly irrational. Similarly making a two-child 
norm conditional for welfare measures  deprives these very sections 
disproportionately for whom these sche mes are meant. The disincentives are 
also anti-women since women in our country do not enjoy the freedom to 
decide how many children they would like to bear. Debarring such women 
from contesting elections or from public employment opportunities makes a 
mockery of policies to empower women, Further, it will provide an impetus 
for sex-selective abortions and female feticide, worsening the already 
deplorable sex ratio in some parts of the country. 
t would therefore, request you that while formulating State specific 
population policies, the State Government may kindly keep the conceptual 
framework of National Population Policy in view. Those States which have 
included coercive measures and disincentives in their State Population 
Policies may undertake a review of their Policy documents to bring them in 
line with the National Population Policy, 2000, with regard to the strategies 
for population stabilization. The Policy is based on the commitment for 
improving the quality of lives that people lead without any coercion or 
controlling the option of the citizens. In this regard, you may like to take the 
help of National Level Resource Committee constituted by this Department. 
A copy of the Order relating to his Committee is enclosed. 
As Population Policy is an issue of vital concern for the overall socio-
economic development of the States and is  not merely a health related issue, 
I would request you to assume a leadership role in formulation of the policy 
framework. 
I am enclosing an article of Prof. Amartya Sen, Noble Laureate and a note 
prepared by us on two-child norm and on incentives and disincentives, which 
you may find useful. 
Yours faithfully,

Development of ROSNI 
514. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister 
of HEALTH AND FAMILY.,WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a new technique for curbin g infertility among couples named 
ROSNI (Round Spermatid Nuclear Injection) has been developed, in the field 
of Test Tube Baby Technique and Artifi cial Reproductive Technology at the 
Jaipur Fertility and Microsurgery Research Centre; 
(b) if so, the details of the technique and how far it has tested to be 
successful; and 
(c) the steps being taken to promote the technique? 
117 

 
RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) "ROSNI" or Round 
Spermatid Nuclear Injection Technique is a new technique in the field of test 
tube baby and this artificial reproductive technology has been developed at 
Jaipur Fertility and Microsurgery Research Centre. ROSNI offers alternative 
solutions for men with non-obstructive azoosoermia and testicular foci of 
spermatogenesis up to round spermatid stage. In this technique, the eggs are 
retrieved from female partner, after ovulation induction under transvaginal 
sonography guidance, like any routine In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF) procedure. 
At the same time, testicular issue is taken from husband and round spermatids 
(haploid) nuclei are extracted from if and injected directly in to the oocytes tike 
intracytoplamic sperm in jection (ICSI) technique. The fertilized egg or 
embryo is transferred back to uterus on day 3 of retrieval. Confirmation of 
pregnancy is done by blood test (S. BhCG) after 15 days. 
However, the fertilization rate as well as pregnancy rate (about 5%) using 
round spermatids is far less than that reported by conventional "Test Tube 
Baby Technique". Moreover, the safety of using round spermatozoa in this 
technique is still being debated. Some  reports suggest th at the spermatids 
{recovered from patients with complete  spermiogenesis failure) are often 
deficient in the factor(s) responsible for oocyte activation which could result 
in abnormal fertilization and the impairment of preimplantation and post-
implantation development of foetus. Besides this, there are other reports which 
have also expressed concern about th e possible health hazards for children 
resulting from the use of spermatids for assisted reproduction. 
The first report of success by this proc edure came in 1995 (Tesarik et al, 
1995 Tesarik & Mendoza, 1996). However, this technique has not been 
universally accepted and certain countr ies have banned this technique, e.g. 
U.K. 
In the light of the available data, it is essential to go slow in using the 
technique ROSNI to treat infertility.

UPON hearing counsel the Court made the following 
ORDER 
We have heard the learned counsel for the petitioner. The challenge is to the 
validity of the petitioner. The challenge is to the validity of the legal services 
authority (Amendment) Act, 2002 (in short the 'Act') whereby a new Chapter 
6(A) has been inserted relating to pre-litigation conciliation and settlement. It 
is quite apparent that this chapter has been enacted as being complementary to 
Section 89 of the code of civil Procedure, 1908 (in short the 'Code') which is a 
new provision enacted and implemented with effect from 1" July, 2002. 
We have gone through the provisions of the said Capter which contemplete 
the setting up of permanent Lok Adalats for deciding disputes in which 
public utility services is one of the matters involved. It is quite obvious that 
the effort of the legislature is to d ecrease the work load in the Courts by 
resorting to alternative disputes resolution. Lok Adalat is a mode of dispute 
resolution which has been in vogue since over two decades. Hundreds of 
thousands of cases have been set tled through this mechanism and is 
undisputedly a fast means of dispensation of justice. The litigation is brought 
to a quick end with no further appeals or anguish to the litigants. The 
constitution of the Perm anent Lok Adalats mech anism contemplate the 
judicial officer or a retired judicial officer being there aiongwith other 
persons having adequate experience in the public utility services. 
We do not find any constitutional infirmity in the said legislation. The Act 
ensures that justice will be available to the litigant speedily and impartially. 
We do emphasis that the persons who are appointed on the 
154 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Permanent Lok Adalats should be persons of integrity and adequate 
experience. Appropriate ru!es, inter alia in this regard, no doubt will have to 
be framed, if not already in place. 
We upheld the validity of the said Act and hope the "Permanent Lok 
Adalats will be set up at an early date. The Lok Adalats are enacted to 
primarily bring about settlement amongst the parties. The parties are normally

563. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: Will the Minister of SHIPPING be

for port services as they feel the tariff should be determined by market forces; 
(c) whether the private ports and Maritime Development Council have 
also opposed the move to bring minor ports under Tariff Authority for Major 
Ports; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING (SHRI 
SU. THIRUNAVUKKARASAR): (a) to (d) The Committee headed by Shri C. 
Babu Rajiv did not recommend bringing minor Ports under the jurisdiction of 
Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP). However, while considering the issue 
relating to 'Uniformity in Port Tariffs', the Parliamentary Standing Committee

Committee held that it is clearly a discrimination towards the Major Ports of 
the country, adversely affecting the competitive environment. The 
Committee, therefore, recommended that there should be the same regulation 
for all ports or, if that was not possible, then major ports should have liberty 
to fix port tariff on their own. The matter was also discussed in the 4*^ 
meeting of the Maritime States Development Council (MSDC) which 
recommended that a Tasl< Force be constituted by the Ministry of Shipping to

ports and comparable non-major ports may be subjected to similar regulations.

appellate authority as well as extending its jurisdiction to non-major ports.

Levy of user charges by States 
603. SHRl PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have asked States to levy user 
charges as part of an exercise to help States to augment resources for 
undertaking urban infrastructure projects; 
(b) whether this levy of user char ges is a precondition for accessing 
Central aid for urban reforms; and 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
(c) if so, the aims of this scheme and the objectives for which it is 
designed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): 
(a) to (c) Urban Development is a State s ubject. It is, therefore, for the States 
to levy user charges to augment resources for undertaking urban 
infrastructure projects. However, in-order to accelerate the pace of sustainable 
urban development, Central Government announced the following new 
tools:— 
(i)   Urban Reforms Incentive Fund (URIF). 
(ii)   City Challenge Fund (CCF). 
(iii)   Pooled Finance Development Scheme (PFDS). 
URIF has been set up to provide reform  linked assistance to states in the 
following areas:— 
(i) Repeal of Urban Land Ceiling and Regulation Act at the State 
level by Resolution; 
(ii) Rationalization of Stamp Duty in phases to bring it down to no 
more than 5% by the end of the Tenth Plan period; 
(iii) Reform of Rent Control Laws to remove rent control so as to 
stimulate private investment in rental housing. 
(iv)   Introduction of computerized processes of registration; 
(v) Reform of Property Tax so that it may become a major source of 
revenue of urban local bodies, and arrangements for its effective 
implementation so that collection efficiency reaches at least 85% 
by the end of 10% Plan period; 
(vi) Levy of reasonable user charges by Urban Local Bodies with the 
objective that full cost of Oper ation & Maintenance is collected 
by the end of the Tenth Plan period; and 
(vii) Introduction of double entry sy stem of accounting in urban local 
bodies. 
CCF is an incentive based facility that will support cities to fund transitional 
costs of moving towards sustainable & creditworthy institutional systems of 
municipal management & service delivery. It will assist in the partial financing 
of the cost of developing an economic reform programme & financially viable 
projects to be undertaken by urban local bodies. 
198 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
PFDS is meant to provid e credit enhancement to assist local bodies to

STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER  
Attack on Raghunath Mandir In Jammu on 24** Novamber, 2002 
THE DEPTY PRIME MINISTER IN CHARGE OF THE MINISTRY OF 
HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L, K. ADVANI): Sit, terrorist groups being mentored 
from across the international border/Line of Control in J&K have struck once 
again  this time on the famous Raghunath Temple of Jammu. These terrorists 
have demonstrated their total lack of concern for the overwhelming yearning 
for peace demonstrated by the people of JSK when they braved violence and 
exercised their right of vote in the rec ent Legislative Assembly elections. The 
terrorists have simultaneously shovwi their disdain for internationaf opinion 
and the efforts of various countries which have been trying to apply momi and 
diplomatic pressure to end cross tMrder terrorism in India. 
In the last three days, there have been a series of attacks by 
terrorists, chief among wh'ch were a suicidal attack on the CRPF Camp at 
Pamposh Hotel Complex. Srinagar on 22"^ November and tatgeting the 
Jammu-bound Army cdnvoy through an lED near Jawahar Tunnel on 23"^ 
November, These and the present attack on Raghunath Temple makes one 
speculate whether it is a mere coincidenc e that this spate of terrorist incidents 
has occurred just when the process of government formation has been 
completed in Pakistan. The spurt of vi olence also follows the release by the 
Government of Pakistan of the chief of LET. Hafiz Mohammad Sayeed- After 
his reteas? he vowed to continue the 'Jehad' in J&K and gave a public call to 
step uo terrorist violence in J&K. 
Monitoring of the communication network of terrorists indicates that 
the Jammu attack is the handiwork of  Al Mansooran. which is a cover 
organtsation of the Lashkar-e-Toiba. 
The present incident has been aimed at innocent civilians at a public 
place of worship. Earlier, in March th is year also, the terrorists had carried out 
an attack on the Temple in which five pe rsons were killed. The three terrorists 
responsible for that assault were also eliminated.

[25 November. 2002) RAJYA SABHA 
According to reports, late on Sunday evening two terrorists appeared 
at Ragliunatli Mandir Chowk, Jammu. One of them forced entry into the 
Mandir Complex and hurled grenades t hereby creating panic in the area. 
People started running helter skelter. Ta king advantage of the situation, the 
terrorists mingled with the crowed and entered Raghunath Mandir, When 
confronted by a CRPF constable, the terronsts opened indiscriminate fire 
killing him on the spot and causing cas ualties to a number of others including 
civilians. However, the Pujaris managed to close the sanctum sanctorum 
forcing one of the terrorist to take shelter on the periphery of the sanctum 
sanctorum. The CRPF personnel guarding the temple laid a cordon to prevent 
the escape of this terrorist. The operation at the Raghunath Temple 
culminated with the elimination of the terro rist hiding in the Mandir late on 24"' 
November evening. 
At the same time, the second terrorist escaped in the melee towards 
Panjbakhter Road, opened fire and lobbed grenades. This place is located 
just a few hundred meters away from Raghunatn Temple where another Shiv 
Mandir called Rupaya Wala Mandir is located. Alert JKP personnel closed the 
doors of the Shiv Temple preventing entry of the terrorist. The terrorist 
resorted to firing from a congested area adjoining this Shiv Mandir. The area 
was then cordoned off and this terrorist was killed this morning (25"' 
November). 
The State Government has intimated that at the time  of the earlier 
terrorist attack on the Raghunath Mandir in March, 2002, the complex was 
guarded by 2/8 Guard of SSB personnel be sides local police for frisking etc. 
which was subsequently replaced by one Platoon of CRPF. This was further 
augmented by deploying one section each  of the CRPF at Raghunath Chowk 
and Hari Market - entry points of the temple. In addition. local police are 
deployed also at various check points in and around the temple. In this terrorist 
attack on 24'" November, 12 persons, including one poiiceman. one 
CRPFyaivan and one militant were killed. Around 52 persons sustained 
injuries. One more injury to a Dy. S.P. occurred in Ihe Shiv Mandir incident of

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS {SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to {d) With the dismantling of Administered Pricing Mechanism 
(APM) In the petroleum sector effective 1st April 2002, the prices of petrol 
and diesel have been decontrolled. The Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) are 
now fixing the prices of these products after taking into account the 
international market. 
As per the existing arrangement between OMCs and domestic 
refineries, the former pay to the latter import parity prices for petrol and diesel, 
revised on fortnightly basis in line with the international oil market. OMCs, in 
turn, revise the domestic consumer prices of these products on fortnightly basis. 
During the months of October'02 and November '02, OMCs increased the 
prices on 1 st October '02 and 17th October '02 and reduced the prices on 16th 
November '02. 
Post APM, the prices of petrol and diesel would be market determined and 
the Government does not intend to regulate the pricing of petrol and diesel 
except to see that oil companies do not indulge in profiteering.

Statement 
The major recommendations as contained in the consultation paper 
inter-alia are as under:— 
(i) Certain non-core functions of the l-T Department including 
allotment of PAN, data entry etc. may be outsourced. 
(ii) A Tax Information Network (TIN) may be created which will 
receive the Return of Tax Deducted at Source and other 
information in a digitized form on behalf of tax administrators. 
Through networking of Banks with TIN, payments may be 
received online and the designate d banks may issue refunds. 
Challans orTDS certificates may not be required to be enclosed 
with the return. 
(iii) Various Administrative and Financial Powers may be delegated to 
the Central Board of Direct Taxes. 
(iv) The basic exemption limit may be  increased to Rs . 1,00,000 with 
removal of almost all exemptions on personal taxation including 
(a) tax rebate under section 88 relating to investment in NSC, 
EPF, GPF, PPF, tax saving units of mutual funds, insurance 
premia paid, repayment of housing loan, infrastructure bonds 
etc., (b) rebates under sections 888 and 88C available to senior 
citizens and women, (c) Deductio n under section SOL relating 
to dividend and interest, (d) exemption under section 10 in 
respect of interest income from bonds, securities, debentures etc.

currency notes, scaling up of vigilance by the Border Security Force/Custom 
Authorities to prevent smuggling of fake currency notes into the country, 
incorporation of special security feat ures in high denomination notes and

Doordarshan for the benefit of public. A High Level Committee (HLC) of 
experts, with representations from Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Home 
Affairs, National Security Council Sectt., Reserve Bank of India and the Bank 
Note Printing Presses, constituted to examine the whole gamut of problems 
caused by circulation of fake currency has submitted its report. Based on the 
recommendations of the HLC, some additional security features have been

counterfeiting extremely difficult.

1. The primary object or principal business of which is the transaction of the

India for grant of licence to carry on banking business within three months. 
Further, even after 1966, as and when the owned funds of a primary credit 
society reaches Rs. one lakh, it has to necessarily apply to the RB! for a licence,

Economic growth 
668. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND  
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the average economic growth in the past three 
years has been only 4 per cent compared to 7.5 per cent in the years 1994—
97; 
(b) whether Government have identified the causes for this poor 
performance; and 
(c) if so, the strategies drawn up to improve performance? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) As per 
the Central Statistical Organisation, the average growrth in Gross Domestic Product 
(GDP) at constant {1993-94 prices) during 1994-95 to 1996-97 was 7.5 per 
cent compared with 5.1 per cent during 1999-2000 to 2001 -02. 
(b) The lower growth in GDP during 1999-2000 to 2001-02 has been 
mainly due to lower average growth in agriculture and allied sector, mining and 
quarrying as also in some of the service sectors. 
(c) The Government is conscious of the need for higher economic 
growth. The Union Budget for 2002-03 adopted a six-pronged strategy, inter-
atia. emphasising continuation of agricultural and food economy reforms, 
enhancement of public and private investment in infrastructure, strengthening the 
financial sector and capital markets, deepening structural reforms and regenerating 
industrial grov/th. The various reform measures are expected to have a positive 
effect on the growth of the economy.

September 2001, RBI announced the guidelines in terms of which banks were

700. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state; 
(a) the reasons for SEBI allowing preferential allotment by the

preferential allotment route by the promoters and why the same has failed to 
protect the interest of shareholders of such companies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS {SHRIANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) 
Companies can make preferential issu es under the provisions of the 
Companies Act, 1956, provided they have obtained a shareholders' resolution 
regarding the quantum of shares, the price at which the issue is to be made, the 
allottees (who may be promoters) etc. They are not required to make any reference 
to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) or to seek its approval 
for making a preferential issue.

compaies are not compromised on account  of preferential issues, the SEBI 
(Disclosure and Investor Protection) Guidelines 2000, inter-alia, prescribe 
the pricing formula, mandatory disclosures In the explanatory statement, lock 
in of shares, disclosures regarding utilisaton of proceeds from the preferential
