Inter-State Water Crisis 
749. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact, that India has enough water to take care of every 
State need; 
(b) if so. the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that inter-State crisis over the use of this water 
resource is increasing every-year; and 
(d) if so, the details of the steps, Government propose to take to solve 
the inter-State river water disputes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) As per the 
latest assessment {1993) made by Central Water Commission (CWC), the average 
annual water availability in the river-system of the country is assessed at 1869 
Billion Cubic Meter (BCM). The availability of water is assessed river basin-
wise. The per capita water availability in  the year 2001 is 1820 cubic metre 
per year on a national level. The lowest per capita average availability of 
water in the country is estimated as 298 cubic metre annually in Sabarmati basin 
and the highest per capita average availability of water in the country is 
estimated as 16,990 cubic metre 
163 

RAJYA  SABHA [26 November, 2002] 
annually in Minto River Basins Draining into Bangladesh & Mayanmar 
followed by 13,636 cubic metre annually In Brahmaputra-Barak Sub-basin. 
(c) The Ravi and Beas Water Dispute between the State of Punjab, 
Haryana and Rajasthan and Cauvery Water Disputes between the States of 
Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and P ondicherry were referred to Tribunals 
under the provisions of Inter State Water Dispute (ISWD) Act, 1956 in April, 
1986 and June 1990 respectively. The Central Government in 2002 has 
received requests under Section 3 of the said Act from the States of Goa and 
Karnataka respectively for referring to the Tribunals the disputes relating to 
sharing of water of Mahadayi/ Madevi river and sharing of surplus water of 
Krishna river for adjudication and decision. 
(d) The Central Government endeavours to resolve the dispute by 
negotiations, failing which the dispute is referred to a Tribunal at the request of party 
States as per the provision of ISWD Act, 1956 for adjudication. The said Act 
has been amended on March 28, 2002 to provide for time-bound adjudication of 
disputes by the Tribunals. Also as pe r the amended Act, the decision of the 
Tribunal, after its publication in the Official Gazette, shall have the same force as 
an order or decree of the Supreme Court. 
Sustainable Water Security System 
750. SHRI H. K. JAVARE GOWD A: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the steps Government propose to take for developing 
a sustainable water security system for the country; and 
(b) what would be the cost for conservation of water and its 
sustainable and equitable use for dom estic agricultural and industrial 
purposes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) 
National Water Resources Council has adopted the revised National Water 
Policy-2002 in April 2002 wherein, emphasis has been laid on the 
conservation and preservation of water resources, optimal utilization of the 
existing water resources infrastructure , development of new resources with 
active participation of all the stakeholders in 
164 

[26 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
various facets of water resources ma nagement. The policy further provides 
for inter basin transfer of river w/ater from the flood prone areas to the water 
scarce areas. These measures aim at sustainable and equitable development of 
water resources and water security in the country. 
There is an average annual precipita tion {Including snowfall) of 4000 
Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) in the country. Out of this, the annual average 
flow in the river systems of the count ry Is 1869 BCM. Th e utillzable surface 
water is assessed as 690 BCM and the annual replenlshable ground water 
resource Is about 432 BCM. Out of which 605 BCM is being presently 
utilised through Su rface and Ground water resources. Besides, additional 
water will be used through inter-basin transfers as envisaged in the National 
perspective Plan for water resources development. Utilisation of balance 
water is to be done through various schemes of water resources development 
and its conservation. Water being a State subject. Plans tor conservation of 
water and its sustainable development are formulated, planned and executed 
by the State Governments as per their requirements and priorities from their 
own resources. The cost of development and conservation of water for 
diverse purposes through conventional and other methods has not been 
worked out.

States' Share on Water Management 
753.   SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether share of States spending on water management is declining 
sharply, as reported in the Economic Times dated the 5th August, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether there has been considerable less rainfall during the current 
year; 
(c) if so, whether this has further aggravated the shortage of water in 
many States; 
(d) whether the National Water Policy adopted by Government has failed 
to provide right climate for private sector participation in this sector; and 
(e) if so, the steps Government propose to take to implement the other 
recommendations of the National Water Policy to meet the water shortage? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY); (a) There has been a 
consistent increase in the plan-wise outlays (in absolute terms) for water 
management that encompasses Irrigation, command area development and flood 
control activities. However, percentage share of public investment including States' 
share in water management in relation to the total investment has consistently 
declined from 23% in the first plan to about 6% in the Ninth Plan as indicated 
in the statement (Seebelow). 
(b) The year 2002 was the firs t all-India drought year after a continuous 
spell of 14 good monsoons that followed the previous all-India drought year of 
1987. The monsoon rainfall (June-September) for the 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [26 Movember, 2002] 
country as a whole was 19% below normal. 29% area of the country 
experienced drought conditions with 19%  area under moderate category and 
10% under severe category. 
(c) The average per capita water availability at present in the country is 1820 
cubic metre per year as against the international criteria of annual water 
availability of less than 1000 cubic metre per capita which is considered as 
scarcity condition. However, due to the spatial variability of rain in the country 
and also because of variation in population density, per capita average annual 
availability of water in different basins presently varies from 13, 636 cubic 
metre in Brahmaputra-Barak basin to 298 cubic metre in Sabarmati basin. The 
temporal variability in the rainfall also creates temporary scarcity of water in 
certain years. The less rainfall during the current year has resulted in water 
shortage in certain parts of the country where rainfall was for below normal. 
(d) The National Water Policy, 2002 provides that private sector 
participation should be encouraged in planning, development and 
management of water resources projects for diverse uses wherever feasible. 
(e) The National Water Policy, 2002 provides that each State shall 
formulate its own State Water Policy back ed with an operational Action Plan 
in a time bound manner, say in two years to achieve the desired objectives of 
the Policy including meeting the water shortage. After adoption of the 
National Water Policy in April, 2002, several steps have been taken for Its 
implementation.These include inter-ministerial meetings with Central and State 
Governments, interaction with Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) and 
institutions concerned with the water sector. A series of seven regional Workshops 
was also organised by the Ministry of Water Resources at various places in the 
country during August to October, 2002 for continued deliberations with the 
NGOs, water experts and professionals. The Action Plan will be placed in the 
Conference of Water Resources and Irrigation Ministers of States and Union 
Territory Administrations for its consider ation and thereafter sent to all State 
Governments and concerned Central Ministries for implementation.

Management of Water Resources 
755. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased state: 
(a) whether a fresh review has been undertaken to assess the availability 
of utilisable water and its demand in the country in the wake of recent drought in 
several parts of the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that with the present rate of growth in population the 
demand for utilisable water for domestic industrial and agricultural purposes 
would out-strip its supply, reaching critical famine conditions by 2025 A.D.; and 
(d) if so, the details of the long term plans drawn up to ensure better 
management of water resources and other research based practical and 
affordable solutions? 
170 

[26 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) No, Sir. As 
per the latest assessment made the utilisable surface water is assessed as 690 Billion 
Cubic Metre (BCM), the annual replenishable ground water resource is about 
432 BCM, totaling to 1122 BCM. This utilizable flow is out of total availability 
of water of 1869 BCM. On an average the total water resources availability in 
the country remains the same although the spatial and temporal variability of 
rain in the country creates temporary scarcity of water in certain years. The 
drought conditions in certain parts of the country during the current year is a 
result of less rainfall this year. 
(c) Owing to increase in population, urbanization and better living 
standards the demand of water for diverse uses has been estimated for the year 
2025 AD as 1093 BCM out of which 73 BCM is for domestic. 23 BCM is for 
industrial, 910 BCM is for irrigation (Agriculture), 15 BCM is for energy and 72 
BCM is for other uses. The projected demand of water for the year 2025 will be 
possible to meet by exploiting almost all the 1122 BCM of utilizable water by 
conventional means. 
(d) Through concerted efforts of State Governments, an irrigation 
potential of approximately 95.40 million hectares has been created by the end of 
9th Five Year Plan. This has been possible due to construction of 3596 major 
and medium projects providing 177 BCM of storage of rain water. Another 
207.7 BCM of storage is likely to be created through ongoing and proposed projects. 
To help the State Governments in their efforts to harness the water from natural 
resources and accelerate creation of irrigation potential by early completion of 
ongoing schemes, Government of Indi a has launched Accelerated Irrigation 
Benefits Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97. Under the programme, financial 
assistance In the form of central loan is being extended to State Governments to 
help them complete the ongoing irrigation projects in a time bound manner so that 
the benefits could accrue at the earliest. Accordingly, the Central Loan Assistant 
(CLA) amounting to Rs. 8480 crore to the State Governments have been provided 
under AIBP upto end of 2001-02. An outlay of Rs. 2800 crore has been 
provided for the year 2002-03. An amount of Rs. 594.75 crore has been released 
duhng current year upto 31.10.2002. 
Government of India is also promoting rain water harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of ground water and 
roof-top rain water han/esting under the sectoral reform project of 
171 

RAJYA  SABHA [26 November, 2002] 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Program me urxier the Ministry of Rural 
Development, for which technical and financial assistance Is provided to the 
State Governments and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water 
Board has taken up a Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to 
Ground Water" on pilot basis under which 174 schemes have been approved in 
various parts of the country during Ninth Five Year Plan. The scheme has been 
proposed to be extended during the Tenth Five Year Plan. Assistance is also being 
extended to State Governments under Command Area Development (CAD) 
programme for bridging the gap between potential created and utilized. An 
expenditure of Rs. 764.42 crore has been incurred during Ninth Five Year Plan 
under CAD programme and an outlay of Rs. 202 crore has been earmarked for the 
year 2002-03. 
For meeting future requirements of water as a long term measure, 
National Water Development Agency have formulated National Perspective Plan for 
water resources development which envi sages interlinking between various 
Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for transfer of water from surplus basins 
to water deficit basins which will accrue benefits of drinking water supply, 
irrigation, hydro-power, flood control, navigation, fisheries, salinity and 
pollution control etc.

Funds allocated for rain water harvesting in Karnataka 
762. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the details about popularization of rain water harvesting schemes in the 
country; 
(b) the amount so far spent during the last two years on rain water 
harvesting; and 
(c) the details of amount, if any, allotted to the State of Karnataka for 
popularization of rain water harvesting during the last two years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CH AKRAVARTY): (a) The Central 
Ground Water Board (CGWB), under the Ministry of Water Resources, has taken 
the following steps to popularize rain water harvesting in the country: 
(i) Implementation of a Central Sector  Scheme for Study of Recharge to 
Ground Water in the country during the IX Five Year Plan at a cost of Rs. 23.48 
crore. (ii) Circulation of Manual and Guide on Artificial Recharge of Ground 
Water incorporating various modern techniques of rain water harvesting to the 
States/Union Territories, for adoption. (Hi) Organisation of mass awareness 
programmes and training courses on rain water han/esting and artificial recharge 
of ground water, (iv) Launching of a website on Roof Top Rain Water 
Harvesting (www.cgwbindia.com) to ma ke aware and educate the public 
about various techniques of harvesting rainwater and store it for future use. (v) 
Providing technical guidance to individuals/organization/ industries to adopt 
efficient recharge system throughout the country, (b) and (c) The Central Ground 
Water Board has implemented a Central Sector Scheme on 'Study of Recharge to 
Ground Water' during ;he IX Five Year Plan at a cost of Rs. 23.48 crore. A total 
number of 155 projects at a cost of Rs. 20.23 crore were taken up during 2000-
2001 and 2001 -2002. Out of the above, 2 projects at a cost of Rs. 28.75 lakh 
were taken up in Karnataka. These projects are at various stages of 
implementation. An 
177

amount of Rs. 16.25 lakh was spent during these two years for organizing training 
and mass awareness programmes in the coun try. Out of this, Rs. 60,000/- was 
spent in Karnataka. 
MNC's right over water 
†763. SHRI JANESHWAR IV1ISHRA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Multi National Companies are acquiring the 
rights over water instead of that of the community; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Central Government and other State 
Governments are also contemplating to privatize this sector; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) No, Sir. 
The rights over water are not being given to Multi National Companies. The 
National Water Policy envisages inolvement of stakeholders, Non-
Governmental Organisations and the private sector in planning, development 
and management of water sources. As laid down in the policy, the water 
supply and sewerage services in some of the mega cities are being 
contemplated by some of the State Governments to be given to the Corporate 
Sector on lease basis for management and improvement of service efficiency.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER

water short areas by transfer from other areas including transfers from

Depletion of Groundwater in Andhra Pradesh 
DR. T SUBBARAMI REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the mapping done 
by the National Remote Sensing Agency to find out the ground water prospects 
for Andhra Pradesh, indicates that ground water reservoirs are fast depleting. 
Sir, NRSA took 300 aerial maps of the State and discovered that Andhra 
Pradesh is a 'problematic' State owing to its rocky terrain. This is the first time that 
a combination of satellite inputs and ground inputs have been used for mapping 
which is more accurate than the ground inputs used in the past. The only 
solution to improve the ground water level is to take up a massive programme for 
recharging the ground water Sir, NRSA has prepared 1723 maps for six States, 
including 300 maps for Andhra Pradesh. The Agency has mapped Andhra 
Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and 
Jharkhand. The study revealed that all the seven States are problematic as 
regards the ground water situation because of rocky terrain. These maps have 
been prepared under a three-year programme, s ponsored by the Ministry of 
Rural Development, in technical collaboration with the ISRO. Therefore, the 
Ministry should take up a massive programme tor recharging the ground water in 
the State of Andhra Pradesh and in other six States urgently to solve the ground 
water problem.

proportions, engulfing the investors more vigorously than in the days of Harshad

Prevention of Thaiassaemia in the country 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Bengal): Sir. Thaiassaemia is a 
dreaded genetic disease. According to the World Health Organisation (1997) 
statistics, about 26,000 children in India are born every year, with this disease. It is 
estimated that one-fourth of the total Thalassamic babies in the world are born in 
our country. The cost of treatment of each patient is roughly estimated at Rs. 1.5 
Rs.-1.75 lakhs per annum. 
To eradicate this disease, pre-marriage counselling is the only 
alternative. If a carrier of this disease does not marry another carrier of this 
disease, then prevention can become very simple. Thaiassaemia can be 
fought only with awareness and resulting consciousness. Due to lackofawarness 
in our country, the number of affected births is regularly increasing. Many of the 
Mediterranean coutries have eradicated the disease through awareness 
programmes and by enacting suitable legislation, compulsory blood examination 
of both males and females before marriage.

The Govenment of India should also initiate massive popular awareness 
campaigns to eradicate this disease.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Implementation of rural development schemes 
*121.    SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: 
SHRI MOOLCHANDMEENA†: 
 Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether some State Governments are facing problem of financing the 
centrally sponsored schemes; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) how Government propose to solve the problem? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI ANNASAHEB M. K. PATIL): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Guidelines of the major rural development programmes of the 
Ministry of Rural Development namely, Sampooma Grameen Rozgar Yojana 
(SGRY), Swamjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), Indira Awaas Yojana 
(IAY) and Watershed Programmes, stipulate that State Governments should 
provide their predetermined share. Many States have not been providing 
matching share for the Programmes of the Ministry of Rural Development. 
(b) A Statement showing the shortfall in release of State's share by different 
States during 2001 -02 for the major allocation based Programmes (SGRY, SGSY 
and I AY) is given in the Statement (See below). 
(c) The Ministry has-been impressing upon the States to release full State's 
share under different programmes, as shortfall in release of State's- share results 
in proportionate cuts in Central releases. The Ministry, in exceptional cases, 
has released funds, on assurance from th e States regarding release of State's 
share, so that the implementation of programmes meant for the poorest of the 
poor is not adversely affected. 
 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri 
Moolchand Meena.

Vishnuprayag and Srinagar Hydro-power Projects 
†* 122. PROF. ALKA BALRAM SHATRIYA: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that agreements for Vishnuprayag and Srinagar hydro-
power projects of Uttaranchal are proposed to be signed afresh; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whemer Uttar Pradesh's demand for 12 per cent free power is the main 
hurdle in the implementation of these projects; and 
(d) if so, the details of action Government propose to take to resolve the 
said hurdle? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI AN ANT GANG ARAM GEETE): (a) to 
(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir, 
(b) The Vishnuprayag and Srinagar Hydro-electric schemes were awarded 
for implementation in the private sector by the Uttar Pradesh State Electricity 
Board (UPSEB). Subsequently, consequent to bifurcation of the State of Uttar 
Pradesh and formation of the new State of Uttranchal, these schemes now fall in 
the new State of Uttaranchal though the power to be generated would be supplied 
to Uttar Pradesh. It is in this context that some of the agreements viz., the 
Implementation Agreement, Power Purc hase Agreement (PPA) and Escrow 
Argreement already entered into between the project developers and the UPSEB, 
may have to be suitably amended.

(c) and (d) The issue regarding demand of the Government of the Uttaranchal 
for 12% free power from these two hydro electric generation schemes was 
discussed in a review meeting taken by the Secretary (Power) on 24th June, 2002 
with representatives, inter-alia, from the Government of Uttar Pradesh and 
Uttaranchal. During the meeting, it was informed by the representatives of Uttar 
Pradesh that the State Government of Uttar Pradesh is prepared to give 12% free 
power to Uttaranchal in regard to the Vishnuprayag project, if the transmission 
network for evacuation of this electricity is allowed to be constructed by Uttar 
Pradesh. Government of Uttaranchal have subsequently agreed to this 
proposition. It was also informed by the representative of Government of Uttar 
Pradesh during the said meeting that they propose to take similar action for the 
Srinagar project also. The Government of Uttar Pradesh has informed that 12% 
free power from the Vishn uprayag Hydro-Electric project to Uttaranchal, has 
already been agreed to by them. In regard to the Srinagar project, the decision is 
yet to be taken by the Government of Uttar Pradesh. 
Government of Uttar Pradesh has also informed that the amended PPA and 
amended Escrow and Hypothecation Agreement have been signed in respect of 
the Vishnuprayag project. The finalization of the revised Implementation 
Agreement of this project is under active consideration of the UP Government 
and Uttaranchal Government.

* 128.    SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY : 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA :  
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is fact that there is a sharp dip in exports of readymade 
garments and handicrafts; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and measures proposed for boosting 
exports; and 
(c) the details of relief provided to affected small exporters of garments 
and handicrafts? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI KASHIRAM RANA): (a) to (c) 
No, Sir. As per latest available DGCI and S data, during the period April-July 
2002, readymade garment exports amounted to US$ 1705.0 million recording 
an increase of 4.3% and handicraft exports amounted to US$ 382.5 million 
recording an increase of 3.6%. 
36 

[27November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Government have been taking several steps from time to time to boost 
textile exports including readymade garments and handicrafts. Some of the 
important initiatives are: 
(i) The Government has de-reserved the woven segment of readymade 
garment from the SSI sector. It has also announced the de-reservation 
of knitted segment in the Union Budget 2002-03. 
(ii) Government has imposed a combination of ad-valorem and specific 
duty on 'whichever is higher basis' on import of number of textiles 
and fabrics to safeguard the interest of the domestic industry, 
especially the decentralised sector against cheap imports. 
(iii) In case any unfair trade practi ces come to the notice, action, if 
necessary, under anti-dumping, countervailing measures etc. of the 
WTO could be taken. 
(iv) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
Upgradation of the sector. 
(v) Weaving, processing and garment machinery, which are covered under 
TUFS, hdve been extended the facility  of accelerated depreciation at the 
rate of 50%. Cost of machinery ha s also been reduced through Fiscal 
Policy measures. This further encourages modernisation. (vi) With a view 
to encouraging backward integration, the custom duty on shuttleless looms 
has been brought from 15% to 5%. A programme has also been announced 
to induct 50,000 shuttleless looms and to modernise 2.5 lakh powerlooms 
in the decentralised sector by 2004. 
(vii) Foreign equity participation upto 100% through automatic route has 
been allowed in the textile sector with a few exceptions. 
(viii) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its six branches 
and Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various 
courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of textile 
industry especially apparel in the field of design, merchandising and 
marketing, (ix) To prepare and sensitise the textile industry to conform to 
the ecological requirements of importing countries by providing facilities 
by way of eco-testing laboratories, (x) The Government has launched 
a'Centrally sponsored scheme titled "A pparel Park for Export Scheme" 
for imparting focused thrust for 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2002] 
setting up of apparel manufacturing units of international standards 
at potential growth centres and to give fillip to exports. A provision of 
Rs. 14.5 crore has been made in the B.E. 2002-03 for providing assistance 
under the scheme. 
(xj) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centers, a 
scheme 'Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme' (TCIDS) 
has been launched. A provision of Rs. 15 crores has been made in the 
B.E. 2002-03 for providing assistance under the scheme. 
(xn) With a view to ensure sustainable development of handicrafts sector 
in the country, a new scheme named' Baba Saheb Ambedkar Hastshilp 
Vikas Yojana' has recently been launched. The scheme seeks to 
develop selected artisan clusters into professionally managed self-
reliant community enterprises working on the principle of effective 
member participation and mutual cooperation.

Functioning of Terror Schools in Pakistan 
*131. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the news-item captioned "Pak terror 
school still functioning" which appeared in the Hindustan Times on 15th October, 
2002; 
(b) whether the role of ISI in aiding cross border terrorism has now been 
reoriented and their control over the Pak terror schools/camps grown stronger; 
and 
(c) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTEROF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
CHENNAMANENIVIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Available inputs indicate that Pak Government has withdrawn 
temporary restrictions imposed on the Jehadi outfits in PoK, restored their 
financial/material support and even enhanced assistance to these outfits. Many 
of the militant camps and training centres which were closed or relocated to 
interior areas earlier have reopened and a number of launching bases have been 
reactivated. 
Pakistan has strengthened ISI network to spread terrorism from J&K to 
North-East in the country. Pakistan has also established enduring clandestine 
infrastructure in Nepal and Bangladesh for facilitating ISI to launch anti-India 
operations using Fundamentalist Organisations/local rebels and criminal gangs. 
(c) The Government is aware of the situation and intelligence and security 
forces are keeping a close watch over the situation. In order to deal with the Pak 
ISI menace, the Government has adopted a well-coordinated and multi-pronged 
approach which includes strengthening the border management, galvanizing 
the intelligence machinery, modernization and upgradation of police and security 
forces with advance sophisticated weapons and communication systems etc. 
The Central Government has also been sensitizing the State Governments 
about the threat perception and activities of ISI in the country. As result of 
coordinated action taken by the Central and State security and intelligence 
agencies, a number of Pakistan backed modules have been neutralized in different 
parts of the country.

Killing of Dalits at Jhajjar in Haryana 
834. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: 
SHRI J.CHITHARANJAN: 
SHRI GAYA SINGH: 
SHRI A. VUAYA RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the details of the incident relating to lynching of five Dalits in 
the Jhajjar area of Haryana; and 
(b) what steps have been taken by Central Government to prevent 
recurrence of such incidents and to ensu re safety amongst Dalits of the area 
besides punishing the guilty ones? 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I. D. SWAMI): (a) The Government of Haryana have intimated that the 
incident occurred on the day of Dussehra on October 15, 2002 in which five 
Dalits were killed by a mob near Duleena Police Post in Jhajjar district in Haryana 
following rumours of their involvement in slaughter and skinning of a cow. A 
word spread in the adjoining villages and mob started gathering rapidly and the 
people armed with deadly weapons co ntinued reaching there. The mob was 
extremely violent and started throwing brick-bats and stones on the police 
personnel. Many police officials got in juries. The Executive Magistrate also 
tried his best to pacify the mob but they did not listen to reason. Suddenly a 
violent group of hooligans armed with iron rods and other deadly weapons 
reached there and the mob suddenly moved very fast like flood and pushed the 
police personnel and Magistrates and att acked the alleged cow slaughters with 
iron rods, lathies, stones and bricks-bats etc. after taking them out on the main 
road. There they beat them up and kijled. A case FIR No. 470 dated 15.10.2002, 
u/s 148/149/302/435/332/353/452 IPC PS Jhaijar has been registered and thirteen 
persons have been arrested upto 23.11.2002. The Government of Haryana has 
ordered an enquiry by the Commissioner, Rohtak Division. The Government of 
Haryana has announced an ex-gratia relief of Rs. Five lakhs to the family of 
each deceased and one member of the family of each deceased will be provided 
a job in the Government service. 
(b) "Police and Law and Order" are State subjects as per entries 1 and 2 of 
the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. The prevention, detection, 
registration, investigation and prosecution is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments. However, the Ministry of Home Affairs have issued 
guidelines to the State'Governments from time to time to give more focussed 
attention to improving the administration of the criminal justice system to ensure 
prevention of atrocities against SCs, STs, women and other vulnerable sections 
of society. The guidelines issued by MHA include inter-alia, the sensitization 
of police personnel in the implementation of the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 
1955 and the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes Prevention of Atrocities Act, 
1989, instructions to the police to have a more empathetic approach while dealing 
with the cases of atrocities against them, specifying the scope and responsibility 
of the police personnel investigating such offences, recruitment of sufficient 
number of persons belonging to SCs/STs as police personnel, especially, at the 
cutting edge level, setting up of special cells to deal with such offences, 
programmes for creating awareness among the vulnerable sections of society 
and legal recourse open to them, evaluation of the working of special courts, 
118 

[27 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
identification of atrocity prone areas for prevention of crime, and measures to be taken for 
economic and social rehabilitation of victims of atrocities. The State Governments 
were also requested to undertake a comprehensive review of the effectiveness of the law 
enforcement machinery in tackling the problems faced by members of the Scheduled 
Castes/Schedule Tribes and also take appropriate measures aimed at increasing the 
responsiveness of the law and order machinery. Schemes for Generating Wind and Solar

Electrification of Villages through Renewable Energy Sources 
837. SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA: Will the Minister ofNON-CONVENTIONAL 
ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state. 
(a) whether Government propose to provide power connection to all villages through 
renewable energy sources to attain sustainable development goal; and 
(b) the investments and technology efforts made in this regard ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) and (b) There 
are about 80,000 unelectrified villages in the country. Out of these about 18,000 villages 
are, believed to be in remote and difficult areas which cannot be electrified through 
extension of the conventional grid. The Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy 
Sources proposes to electrify all these villages through renewable energy sources by 
the year 2012. The Ministry accordingly initiated a new programme for village 
electrification in the year 2001 -02. A target for electrifying 5,000 such villages has 
been fixed for the Tenth Plan period. Renewable energy systems like solar 
photovoltaic systems and power plants, small hydro units and biomass gasifiers, which 
use the locally available renewable energy sources, are the most suitable options for 
electrification of remote villages and hamlets. Such systems have already been 
developed indigenously and are being deployed in these villages and hamlets under the 
Ministry's programme. An expenditure of about rs. 20 crores has been incurred by the 
Ministry on this programme during 2001-02. An amount of Rs. 75 crores has been 
provided for this in the budget for 2002-03.

147 

RA JYA SABHA [27 November, 2002] 
Statement 
Summary of three phased approach 
Phase: I Complete the groundwork 
Before proceeding with change, several critical elements need to be in 
place. A structural model for the sector needs to be developed and agreed upon. 
Broad consenses is required to be forged amongst stakeholders such as the 
unions, consumer groups, political parties and the bureaucracy. Several ground 
realities of the sector need to be better understood through objective audits, eg. 
demand and load curves, actual losses and the technical health of generation, 
transmission and distribution assets. Regulators and the regulatory framework 
need strengthening and some changes. A common legal basis for deregulation 
needs to be established. Finally, and perhaps most important, the states need to 
be aligned around a reform agenda that must include an explicit commitment to 
privatisation of the SEBs as well as support for an overall structural model for 
the sector. 
Phase 2: Unbundle, corporatise and privatise 
The restructuring programme must being with reform of the SEBs. 
Following unbundling, the SEB generation capacity should be transferred to its 
natural owners, with a view to ensuring greater operating efficiency. The buyers 
could be in the private or public sector. National transmission should be 
restructured into five regional grids, each with responsibilities for grid operation, 
grid stability and facilitating generator-distributor transactions. The grids should 
be recognised as regulated monopolies, and linked with the necessary 
interconnect protocols. SEB transmission assets should be included in the 
respective regional grids (or at a minimu m, the state transmission grids should 
operate under the instructions of the regional load despatch centres). Distribution 
should be privatised after the technical  audits, following a transparent process 
of bidding and disclosure. At this stage, regulations will need to be introduced 
to allow distribution companies to bid for additional generation capacity. 
Transmission and distribution companies will need to be regulated on the basis 
of performance-linked incentive sharing. 1n addition, fuel supply linkages for 
generators will need to be strengthened. 
148 

[27 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Phase 3: Accelerate the pace of reform 
Introduction of market mechanisms can begin once the unbundling has 
stabilised and efficiency gains have begun to be realised. In the third phase, customer 
choice should be introduced through phased customer eligibility. Wholesaler market 
mechanismus such as on an electricity pool or electricity exchanges can be introduced. 
Further unbundling of the value chain within each sub-sector will also be required, e.g. 
meter reading and plant maintenance. Regulatory mechanisms would also need to be 
further sharpened in this new regime.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
( SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA ) : (a) No privatisation of any power project 
during the last three years have been reported. 
(b) Electricity is a concurrent subject  and distribution is the responsibility 
of the State Government. As per information available, 18 companies are 
engaged in the distribution of power in the public sector and 11 in the private

(c) to (e) Statement II showing T and D losses for the period 1997-98 to 1999-2000 is 
enclosed (see below). It has been noted that reforming States, after detailed studies 
conducted into their operation, have reported higher T and D losses compared to 
figures before restructuring. The apparent increase in reporting of Transmission and 
Distribution losses by most of the SEBs is on account of a more realistic assessment 
of losses within the network. Since a 
149 

    RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2002] 
large number of consumers were unmetered, e.g. agricultural pumpsets, it was 
customary in the past to ascribe part of the losses particularly commercial losses 
(i.e. theft) to consumption by the unmetered segment. With State Regulatory 
Commissions insisting on sample metering of unmetered segments of consumers, 
energy audit etc. the T and D losses now being reported are closer to actual. Even 
now, the figures being reported are estimates on account of the continued existence of 
unmetered categories of consumers. 
Central Electricity Authority have issued Guidelines for reduction of 
transmission and distribution losses in February, 2001. The steps taken to reduce the 
transmission and distribution losses include energy auditing, 100% metering, 
elimination of power theft and strengthening/upgradation of sub-transmission and 
distribution system. Comprehensive Guidelines have also been formulated by a 
Steering Committee of Experts to streamline the sub-transmission and distribution

the total area under cotton cultivation was about ten million hectares. Now it

productivity level has also come down. It is stagnating at 300 kilograms per

Recently, the other day, in response to a question put in the Lok Sabha, it was 
mentioned that the productivity level has come down to 190 kilograms per 
hectare. 
Pest attacks are on the increase due to which farmers are compelled 
to burn all their produce. The Cotton Committee, headed by the 
Commissioner (Cotton) is calculating the required amount of cotton, every 
year as if there has been a surplus position. 
Madam, the international price of cotton is also going down. The 
report of the Hindu Business Review of March says, "After the commercial

SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI : Madam Deputy Chairperson, 
the calling attention brought before us for discussion is not confined to the 
Ministry of Agriculture alone; the spread is more. The hon. Minister of 
Agriculture should not feel that we are going into other areas also. Madam, 
cotton production has been  affected because the fact that, within a 
quinquennium, the production area has declined by 6 lakh hectares from 91 
lakh hectares to 85 lakh hectares; and,  in the same period, that is, between 
1996-97 and 2000-01, the average production, per hectare, has come down to 
191 kg from 265 kg. Earlier, it was called the white gold. Now, it has actually 
become the darkest thing of our nation. Consequently, Tamil Nadu is also 
affected. The area come down to 1.93 lakh hectares from 2.52 lakh hectares. 
My feeling is, the Ministry of Agriculture  alone can't do it. But they have to 
take some initiative for solving the problem. The important issue is regarding 
MSP, and procurement by the Government. If we go through the replies to 
Q.No. 1766 dated 2nd August, 2002, and Q.No. 2082 dated 22" n March, 2002, 
what we understand is that, in the last 5 months, the Cotton Corporation of 
India has purchased only one-lakh-and-forty-thousand bales. This is the 
information we have got from the reply given by the Government itself. This 
is the situation. What is the remedy ? The remedy is different in nature. 
Madam, import duty has been enhanced from 5% to 10%. I would like to 
know whether the Government would come forward to enhance the import 
duty further, taking into consideration the WTO limit. Now, under the WTO 
limit, how much more import duty can we impose? You look into this, and, if 
possible, raise the import duty so as to curb the cotton imports. Would the 
Government do it? This is my first point 
In the case of sugar, you are providing free transportation from the 
production area to the port. I would like to know whether the^ame kind of 
facility would be provided for cotton exports also. This is my second 
question.

Another point is this. As regards the Modernisation Scheme, there

But, what is the ground reality? Despite this Modernisation Scheme, when the 
textile mills approach the banks, the banks stipulate, "If you have shown

DR. V. MAITREYAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I am thankful to you for 
the opportunity you have given to me. Roughly two weeks from now, the 
people of Gujarat will be electing a new Government, a Government they 
want and a Government they deserve, and. hopefully, that will bring to an end 
the host of controversies that have arisen in the past ten to eleven months. It 
is very essential that elections are held in a peaceful and conducive manner so 
that they will be free and fair. 
The hon. Member, Shri Pranab Mukh erjee, raised the issue of the 
relief work and pointed out certain inadequacies. Shri Arun Jaitleyji 
mentioned that a lot had been done already. I submit that a lot might have 
been done, but, still, probably, a lot more needs to be done. The relief work 
should continue, irrespective of the el ection process. The hon. Member, Shri 
Nilotpal Basu, mentioned about the VHP, the statements made by various 
people, and so on. In the first place, after the announcement of the elections in 
Gujarat, the Vishwa Hindu Parishad could have avoided the organisation of 
the Vijay Yatra. Instead, they went ahead. Worse; when the Yatra was 
banned, the senior VHP leaders mounted a verbal onslaught on the Election 
Commission, which was in bad taste. If the Election Government had received 
Intelligence information from the State Home Ministry, fearing a break-down 
of law and order and fresh communal riot s, if the Yatra took place, then the 
Election Commissioner was right in his decision to ban the Yatra. But the 
question arises: Could he not have requested the Central Government or the 
State Government, to take appropriate action, instead of directly, himself, 
giving the ban order? Was it within his constitutional powers to do so? That is 
another important question that needs to be addressed. Ultimately, it was the 
statement of the hon. Prime Minister and the hon. Deputy Prime Minister that 
eventually
